Addisons disease affects both the adrenal gland and the medulla. Addisons disease specifically affects the adrenal cortex which secretes aldosterone. Aldosterone regulates salt levels in the blood. In Addisons there is a deficiency in aldosterone meaning there is less salt being absorbed into the blood stream and more potassium being excreted. This causes hypokalaemia. Other symptoms include hyponatraemia due to water loss in sweat. There is also increased thirst, nausea, vomiting and muscle cramps. Treatment of Addisons disease involves replacing the missing hormones. This is done by taking corticosteroid tablets which act like natural cortisol. These help restore the balance of salts in the blood as well as reducing some of the other symptoms. This woman has symptoms of Hyperthyroidism.  The most commonly caused of hyperthyroidism is Graves disease which is an autoimmune condition where the immune system makes antibodies which act like TSH and stimulate the release of thyroid hormones from the thyroid gland.  Carbimazole is prescribed to treat hyperthyroidism. It is converted into a very potent form of thyroid hormone which acts as a competitive inhibitor for iodination of thyroglobulin - reducing the amount of thyroxine released from the thyroid gland.   Insulin is used to treat Hypoglycaemia not Hyperthyroidism.  Hydrocortisone is used to treat Addison's disease not Grave's disease.  Levothyroxine is used to treat hypothyroidism.  T3 is just one of the active forms of thyroid hormone.  Both T4 and T3 are reduced in activity in primary hypothyroidism but levels of TSH are raised. In secondary hypothyroidism both T4 and T3 are reduced in activity but levels of TSH are also reduced.  This was covered in the Case 12 lecture "An introduction to the endocrine system". Neural tube defects are failures in the formation or closure of the neural tube during embryonic development. They lead to abnormalities such as spina bifida (failure of the vertebral column to enclose the spinal cord) and anencephaly (failure of the skull to enclose much of the brain).  The physical manifestation of spina bifida is the presence of a lesion on the lower back, often with a hairy patch associated with it. This is due to failure of the neural tube to close around the spinal cord, leading to exposure of parts of the nervous system. Anencephaly results in the absence of a significant portion of the skull, brain, and related structures. It is usually fatal and ends in stillbirth or death within hours of birth.  Neural tube defects are thought to be caused by a combination of genetic and environmental factors. In particular, maternal dietary intake of vitamin B9, known as folic acid, has been identified as a key preventative factor. Folate deficiency is believed to increase the risk of neural tube defects. Hence, taking folate supplements before conception and during the first trimester of pregnancy is recommended.   Source: http://www.nhs.uk/conditions/spina-bifida/Pages/Introduction.aspx and http://www.cdc.gov/ncbddd/folicacid/neuraltube.html  Also covered in PCS Unit 2 'Development' lecture 'Formation of the Neurular Groove and Tube' slides. Hair cell endings release glutamate in response to depolarisation. This differs from most other neurons where depolarisation causes the release of EPSPs. The reason for this difference is that unlike most other neurons, hair cells have no sodium channels on their membrane and therefore cannot reach threshold by depolarising with sodium ions. The fact that hair cells release glutamate instead of epSPs allows them to reach threshold with a steeper voltage change.
